claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and quantification.

claims.claim: Mature OSNs have on average approximately 36 centrioles.
claims.source: In mature OSNs that had completed centriole migration with centrioles docked at the dendritic knob, each cell had, on average, approximately 36 centrioles (SEM = 1.665; standard deviation = 8.156, n = 24 dendritic knobs from two mice, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and quantification.

claims.claim: Progenitor cells form the majority of centrioles present in the dendritic knob of mature OSNs.
claims.source: These results suggest that progenitor cells form the majority of centrioles present in the dendritic knob of mature OSNs, in keeping with our previously published work (Ching and Stearns, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the centriole counts and supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: On average, 85% of centrioles at a dendritic knob are associated with cilia.
claims.source: We found that, on average, 85% of centrioles at a dendritic knob were associated with cilia (SEM = 2.47; standard deviation = 12.10), with an average of approximately 31 cilia per knob (SEM = 1.455; standard deviation = 7.126).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and quantification.

claims.claim: Mature OSNs have an average of approximately 31 cilia per knob.
claims.source: We found that, on average, 85% of centrioles at a dendritic knob were associated with cilia (SEM = 2.47; standard deviation = 12.10), with an average of approximately 31 cilia per knob (SEM = 1.455; standard deviation = 7.126).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and quantification.

claims.claim: Multiple groups of centrioles can be present within a single dendrite.
claims.source: We first tested whether multiple groups of centrioles could be present within a single dendrite, as suggested by previous TEM results (Heist and Mulvaney, 1968; Mulvaney and Heist, 1971). We imaged immature OSNs using expansion microscopy through the entire thickness of the dendrite. We found that centrioles were positioned in multiple groups within the same dendrite (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The dendrite does not fully extend prior to centriole migration.
claims.source: We observed centrioles in partially elongated dendrites, indicating that the dendrite does not fully extend prior to centriole migration (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data and Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Centriole groups lag behind the end of the dendrite by as much as 8.4 µm.
claims.source: The leading portions of the dendrites had a variety of growth cone morphologies, and centriole groups lagged behind the end of the dendrite by as much as 8.4 µm (Figure 2B, mean = 3.68 µm, SEM = 0.80 µm, standard deviation = 2.76 µm, n = 12 dendrites, N = 2 animals).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data and Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Microtubules are present both apical to and basal to migrating centrioles.
claims.source: By probing for β-tubulin III (TUBB3), a tubulin isotype expressed primarily in neurons, we observed that microtubules were present both apical to and basal to the migrating centrioles (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data and Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The leading group of centrioles migrates in tandem with dendrite extension.
claims.source: These data indicate that the leading group of centrioles migrates in tandem with dendrite extension and can be followed by lagging groups within the dendrite.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observations of centrioles in partially elongated dendrites.

claims.claim: The fastest moving centriole group moved at approximately 0.18 µm/min.
claims.source: We found that the cells in the excised olfactory epithelium remained intact, with normal nuclear morphology and few delaminating cells over the time course of imaging. Considering net movement over the course of the sequences, centriole groups moved slowly, with the fastest moving at approximately 0.18 µm/min (n = 22 centriole groups, N = 3 animals, Figure 2C, Figure 2—video 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by live imaging data and Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Most centriole groups exhibited net movement in the apical direction.
claims.source: Most centriole groups exhibited net movement in the apical direction (Figure 2C, Figure 2—video 1, n = 14 out of 22 groups observed), although approximately one-third had either net movement in the basal direction or no movement during the imaging period (Figure 2D, Figure 2—video 2, n = 8 out of 22 groups observed).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by live imaging data and Figures 2C and 2D.

claims.claim: Approximately one-third of centriole groups had either net movement in the basal direction or no movement during the imaging period.
claims.source: Most centriole groups exhibited net movement in the apical direction (Figure 2C, Figure 2—video 1, n = 14 out of 22 groups observed), although approximately one-third had either net movement in the basal direction or no movement during the imaging period (Figure 2D, Figure 2—video 2, n = 8 out of 22 groups observed).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by live imaging data and Figures 2C and 2D.

claims.claim: Migrating centrioles lack rootletin signal.
claims.source: We performed expansion microscopy to detect rootletin on centrioles. Strikingly, migrating centrioles lacked rootletin signal (Figure 3A), indicating that these groups are not held together by rootletin-based cohesion fibers.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Migrating centriole groups are not held together by rootletin-based cohesion fibers.
claims.source: We performed expansion microscopy to detect rootletin on centrioles. Strikingly, migrating centrioles lacked rootletin signal (Figure 3A), indicating that these groups are not held together by rootletin-based cohesion fibers.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the absence of rootletin signal on migrating centrioles.

claims.claim: Some centrioles localize singly between migrating groups in immature OSNs.
claims.source: We also observed that migrating centrioles not only move in multiple groups, but that some centrioles are not grouped at all, localizing singly between migrating groups in immature OSNs (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Rootletin is present in centrioles of mature OSNs.
claims.source: The rootletin antibody did detect rootlets associated with centrioles in mature OSNs (Figure 3A), as well as cohesion fibers in tissue culture cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Menco et al., 1978; McClintock et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and Figure 3A.

claims.claim: STIL and SASS6 are present on amplifying centrioles in progenitors.
claims.source: In the olfactory epithelium, both STIL and SASS6 were present on amplifying centrioles in progenitors and localized to the proximal end of newly formed centrioles, supporting the model that these proteins are involved in centriole amplification from rosettes (Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and Figures 3B and 3C.

claims.claim: STIL and SASS6 are retained on at least some migrating centrioles in immature OSNs.
claims.source: Remarkably, STIL and SASS6 are retained on at least some of the migrating centrioles in immature OSNs and are associated with the presumptive proximal end of these centrioles (Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and Figures 3B and 3C.

claims.claim: STIL and SASS6 are absent from centrioles in mature OSNs.
claims.source: In mature OSNs, STIL and SASS6 are absent from centrioles (Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and Figures 3B and 3C.

claims.claim: Immature procentrioles are capable of migrating.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that immature procentrioles are capable of migrating, while the dendritic knob is primarily formed of mature centrioles that lack STIL and SASS6.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the presence of STIL and SASS6 on migrating centrioles.

claims.claim: The dendritic knob is primarily formed of mature centrioles that lack STIL and SASS6.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that immature procentrioles are capable of migrating, while the dendritic knob is primarily formed of mature centrioles that lack STIL and SASS6.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the absence of STIL and SASS6 on centrioles in mature OSNs.

claims.claim: Gamma-tubulin localizes to a diffuse cloud around centriole barrels in progenitor cells and immature OSNs.
claims.source: We first probed for the microtubule nucleator gamma-tubulin using expansion microscopy. In both progenitor cells with amplifying centrioles and in immature OSNs, gamma-tubulin localizes to a diffuse cloud around centriole barrels (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Gamma-tubulin is associated with centrioles in mature, fully ciliated OSNs.
claims.source: In mature, fully ciliated OSNs, gamma-tubulin was also associated with centrioles.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data.

claims.claim: CDK5RAP2 is present in progenitor cells with amplifying centrioles and migrating centrioles in immature OSNs.
claims.source: Both CDK5RAP2 and pericentrin are present in progenitor cells with amplifying centrioles, as well as migrating centrioles in immature OSNs.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Pericentrin is present in progenitor cells with amplifying centrioles and migrating centrioles in immature OSNs.
claims.source: Both CDK5RAP2 and pericentrin are present in progenitor cells with amplifying centrioles, as well as migrating centrioles in immature OSNs.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and Figure 3F.

claims.claim: CDK5RAP2 is present in dendritic knobs.
claims.source: In dendritic knobs, CDK5RAP2 was present, while pericentrin signal decreased.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Pericentrin signal decreases in dendritic knobs.
claims.source: In dendritic knobs, CDK5RAP2 was present, while pericentrin signal decreased.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Groups of migrating OSN centrioles remain associated with microtubule nucleation proteins and PCM.
claims.source: Our data show that groups of migrating OSN centrioles remain associated with microtubule nucleation proteins and PCM, in contrast to the centrioles of many other types of mammalian neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data showing presence of gamma-tubulin, CDK5RAP2, and pericentrin.

claims.claim: In some OSN dendrite tips with multiple centrioles near the apical surface, a single cilium is present.
claims.source: We observed that in some OSN dendrite tips with multiple centrioles, near the apical surface, a single cilium was present (Figure 4A and A′).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and Figures 4A and A'.

claims.claim: In OSNs with a single cilium, distal appendages are present on the centriole at the base of the cilium and not at other centrioles.
claims.source: In OSNs with a single cilium, distal appendages were present on the centriole at the base of the cilium and not at other centrioles (Figure 4A and A′), confirming that an inherent asymmetry in centriole states exists.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and Figures 4A and A'.

claims.claim: An inherent asymmetry in centriole states exists in OSNs.
claims.source: In OSNs with a single cilium, distal appendages were present on the centriole at the base of the cilium and not at other centrioles (Figure 4A and A′), confirming that an inherent asymmetry in centriole states exists.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only one centriole has distal appendages in OSNs with a single cilium.

claims.claim: In OSNs with multiple cilia, many centrioles acquire distal appendages.
claims.source: By contrast, in OSNs with multiple cilia, many centrioles acquired distal appendages, indicating that centriole maturation and remodeling occurred at the apical surface (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Centriole maturation and remodeling occur at the apical surface.
claims.source: By contrast, in OSNs with multiple cilia, many centrioles acquired distal appendages, indicating that centriole maturation and remodeling occurred at the apical surface (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that many centrioles acquire distal appendages in OSNs with multiple cilia.

claims.claim: In progenitor cells, a single, mature, parental centriole segregates to each daughter cell.
claims.source: Based on our previous results regarding centriole amplification (Ching and Stearns, 2020), we hypothesized that in progenitor cells a single, mature, parental centriole segregates to each daughter cell, whereas the newly amplified centrioles remain immature and do not acquire appendages.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the authors' previous work and supported by the current data.

claims.claim: In migrating centrioles, only a single centriole has distal and subdistal appendages.
claims.source: In support of this hypothesis, we found that both in migrating centrioles (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B) and in centrioles in the process of amplification (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), only a single centriole was found to have distal and subdistal appendages.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and Figures 4C and 4—figure supplement 1A-C.

claims.claim: In centrioles in the process of amplification, only a single centriole has distal and subdistal appendages.
claims.source: In support of this hypothesis, we found that both in migrating centrioles (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B) and in centrioles in the process of amplification (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), only a single centriole was found to have distal and subdistal appendages.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The centriole modifications required to make cilia occur after centriole migration during OSN differentiation.
claims.source: These data suggest that the centriole modifications required to make cilia occur after centriole migration during OSN differentiation, and that the already-modified parental centriole is able to make a cilium before all other centrioles.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most centrioles lack appendages during migration but acquire them at the apical surface.

claims.claim: The already-modified parental centriole is able to make a cilium before all other centrioles.
claims.source: These data suggest that the centriole modifications required to make cilia occur after centriole migration during OSN differentiation, and that the already-modified parental centriole is able to make a cilium before all other centrioles.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only one centriole has appendages and forms a cilium in immature OSNs.

claims.claim: In tracheal MMCCs, the parental centriole retains its unique structural characteristics even in mature cells after all cilia form.
claims.source: In tracheal MMCCs, the parental centriole retains its unique structural characteristics even in mature cells after all cilia form (Liu et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: In migrating centrioles, centriolin is present on only one centriole, surrounding that centriole in a subdistal appendage-like pattern.
claims.source: In migrating centrioles, centriolin was present on only one centriole, surrounding that centriole in a subdistal appendage-like pattern (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: In cells in which the parental centriole forms a single cilium, centriolin retains a subdistal appendage-like pattern around the base of the cilium.
claims.source: In cells in which this centriole formed a single cilium, centriolin retained this subdistal appendage-like pattern around the base of the cilium, while other centrioles had acquired single puncta of centriolin (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and Figure 4D.

claims.claim: In mature OSNs with multiple cilia, one centriole is surrounded by centriolin, whereas the other centrioles have only single foci of centriolin.
claims.source: In mature OSNs with multiple cilia, one centriole was surrounded by centriolin, whereas the other centrioles still had only single foci of centriolin, consistent with basal feet as observed in multiciliated epithelial cells (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expansion microscopy data and Figures 4E and 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: In OSNs, the cilium nucleated by the parental centriole has unique structural characteristics compared to the other cilia at the mature dendritic knob.
claims.source: We conclude that in OSNs, as in multiciliated epithelial cells, the cilium nucleated by the parental centriole has unique structural characteristics compared to the other cilia at the mature dendritic knob.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that one centriole retains a unique centriolin pattern in mature OSNs.

claims.claim: Inhibiting microtubule dynamics disrupts centriole migration to the apical surface.
claims.source: Using a novel explant system, we found that inhibiting microtubule dynamics disrupts centriole migration to the apical surface.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by explant culture experiments with paclitaxel treatment.

claims.claim: Cells in the explant cultures can synthesize DNA.
claims.source: We found that EdU, which labels newly replicated DNA, incorporated into nuclei near the basal lamina in the explant, indicating that cells were able to replicate DNA (Figure 5B and C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by EdU incorporation data and Figures 5B and 5C.

claims.claim: Many EdU-positive cells in explants appear to have amplified centrioles.
claims.source: In addition, many of the EdU-positive cells appeared to have amplified centrioles, in accordance with our previous observations (Ching and Stearns, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by EdU incorporation data and the authors' previous work.

claims.claim: The number of EdU-positive nuclei increased from 0.63 nuclei per 100 µm basal length of epithelium at 1 hr to 0.96 nuclei per 100 µm of epithelium at 6 hr.
claims.source: We treated explants with EdU at two time points, 1 and 6 hr post-dissection, and found that the number of EdU-positive nuclei increased from 0.63 nuclei per 100 µm basal length of epithelium to 0.96 nuclei per 100 µm of epithelium (total lengths quantitated = 634.84 µm and 621.52 µm for 1 and 6 hr, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by EdU incorporation data.

claims.claim: Cells in the explant cultures can amplify centrioles.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that cells in the explant cultures can synthesize DNA and amplify centrioles, and that the culture retains its characteristic architecture during the time course.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation of EdU-positive cells with amplified centrioles.

claims.claim: The explant culture retains its characteristic architecture during the time course.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that cells in the explant cultures can synthesize DNA and amplify centrioles, and that the culture retains its characteristic architecture during the time course.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by observations of tissue morphology.

claims.claim: Treatment with paclitaxel for 1 or 6 hr does not affect overall tissue morphology.
claims.source: Treatment with DMSO or paclitaxel for 1 hr or 6 hr did not affect overall tissue morphology, including the actin-rich apical domain (Figure 5D and E).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by observations of tissue morphology in Figures 5D and 5E.

claims.claim: In all conditions, more centriole groups are found in the subapical compartment than in the middle and basal region.
claims.source: In all conditions, more centriole groups were found in the subapical compartment than in the middle and basal region, consistent with previous reports (Mulvaney and Heist, 1971), and suggesting that the explant cultures recapitulate this aspect of in vivo development.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of centriole groups and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Upon treatment with paclitaxel, more centriole groups are found in the subapical and middle/basal compartments.
claims.source: In sum, we found that upon treatment with paclitaxel, more centriole groups were found in the subapical and middle/basal compartments, likely in transit (p=0.0084 by paired permutation test, Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of centriole groups and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: At the 1 hr time point, explants treated with paclitaxel had 1.38-fold more centriole groups in the subapical compartment than control.
claims.source: At the 1 hr time point, explants treated with paclitaxel had only slightly more (1.38-fold) centriole groups in the subapical compartment than control (N = 2 animals, n = 39 and 29 centriole groups, total basal lengths quantitated = 905.37 µm and 988.17 µm for paclitaxel and DMSO, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of centriole groups.

claims.claim: After 6 hr of paclitaxel treatment, the subapical compartment had 2.58-fold more centriole groups compared to control.
claims.source: In contrast, after 6 hr of paclitaxel treatment, the subapical compartment had 2.58-fold more centriole groups compared to control (N = 2 animals, n = 70 and 29 centriole groups, total basal lengths quantitated = 1019.76 µm and 1126.44 µm for paclitaxel and DMSO, respectively, Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of centriole groups.

claims.claim: The accumulation of centriole groups with paclitaxel treatment suggests that microtubule dynamicity is required for centriole groups to complete their progression to the apical membrane.
claims.source: The accumulation of centriole groups with paclitaxel treatment, particularly in the subapical compartment, suggests that microtubule dynamicity is required for centriole groups to complete their progression to the apical membrane.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that paclitaxel treatment leads to accumulation of centriole groups.

claims.claim: Centrioles could take greater than 9.26 hr to traverse an epithelium 100 µm thick.
claims.source: The maximum rate observed indicates that centrioles could take greater than 9.26 hr to traverse an epithelium 100 µm thick.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the maximum migration rate of 0.18 µm/min.

claims.claim: Dividing progenitors require multiple days to give rise to fully mature OSNs.
claims.source: This timing is well within the multiple days required for dividing progenitors to give rise to fully mature OSNs (Rodriguez-Gil et al., 2015; McClintock et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: A parsimonious explanation for how OSNs achieve their final centriole number is that amplification is initiated by rosette formation around the two parental centrioles in progenitor cells, followed by a single mitotic division and centriole disengagement from the rosettes, and further amplification in post-mitotic cells that become OSNs.
claims.source: Based on the new evidence we present here, a parsimonious explanation for how OSNs achieve their final centriole number is that amplification is initiated by rosette formation around the two parental centrioles in progenitor cells, followed by a single mitotic division and centriole disengagement from the rosettes, and further amplification in post-mitotic cells that become OSNs.
claims.evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their data.

claims.claim: OSNs are unique in that they undergo a mitotic division with amplified centrioles, which is then followed by further amplification.
claims.source: OSNs are, to our knowledge, unique in that they undergo a mitotic division with amplified centrioles, which is then followed by further amplification (Ching and Stearns, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous work.

claims.claim: An immature OSN potentially has centrioles of three different ages: the parental centriole, amplified centrioles formed prior to mitosis, and those that may have formed after mitosis.
claims.source: Thus, an immature OSN potentially has centrioles of three different ages: the parental centriole, amplified centrioles formed prior to mitosis, and those that may have formed after mitosis.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the model of centriole amplification in OSNs.

claims.claim: A portion of the amplified centrioles in immature OSNs have undergone the centriole-to-centrosome conversion.
claims.source: We found that some of the amplified centrioles in immature OSNs have nucleation-associated proteins of the PCM, including gamma-tubulin, CDK5RAP2, and pericentrin, consistent with a portion of the amplified centrioles having undergone the centriole-to-centrosome conversion as described in cultured mammalian cells (Wang et al., 2011; Izquierdo et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the presence of PCM proteins on migrating centrioles and supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The final modification of the non-parental centrioles with rootlets, distal appendages, and subdistal appendages/basal feet in OSNs appears to be controlled spatially and/or temporally, by their arrival in the forming dendritic knob.
claims.source: It is interesting that the final modification of the non-parental centrioles with these components in OSNs appears to be controlled spatially and/or temporally, by their arrival in the forming dendritic knob, as they were absent on migrating centrioles in immature OSNs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these components are absent on migrating centrioles but present in mature OSNs.

claims.claim: The presence of a single cilium before formation of the full complement of multiple cilia might enable signaling important for OSN differentiation.
claims.source: The presence of a single cilium before formation of the full complement of multiple cilia might enable signaling important for OSN differentiation, as has been proposed for the primary cilium of MMCCs that precedes multiciliated differentiation (Jain et al., 2010), although we note that Schwarzenbacher et al., 2005 found that the earliest OSN cilia formed lack olfactory receptors.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on comparison to MMCCs and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The earliest OSN cilia formed lack olfactory receptors.
claims.source: The presence of a single cilium before formation of the full complement of multiple cilia might enable signaling important for OSN differentiation, as has been proposed for the primary cilium of MMCCs that precedes multiciliated differentiation (Jain et al., 2010), although we note that Schwarzenbacher et al., 2005 found that the earliest OSN cilia formed lack olfactory receptors.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: In MMCCs, a single parental centriole differs from other centrioles and is associated with a 'hybrid cilium'.
claims.source: This is remarkably similar to the situation in MMCCs in which a single parental centriole also differed from other centrioles and was associated with what was termed a 'hybrid cilium' (Liu et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: In MMCCs of the oviduct, paclitaxel-mediated stabilization of microtubules does not affect centriole biogenesis, but can inhibit centriole migration.
claims.source: In this respect, OSNs are similar to MMCCs of the oviduct, in which paclitaxel-mediated stabilization of microtubules does not affect centriole biogenesis, but can inhibit centriole migration (Lemullois et al., 1988; Boisvieux-Ulrich et al., 1989).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: In the C. elegans ciliated PQR neuron, SAS-5 directly interacts with a dynein light chain (DLC-1/LC8).
claims.source: In the C. elegans ciliated PQR neuron, SAS-5, an ortholog of STIL, directly interacts with a dynein light chain (DLC-1/LC8), suggesting that centrioles may be cargos of cytoplasmic dynein in the dendrite (Li et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The rate of migration for the single centriole in C. elegans neurons is 0.076 µm/min.
claims.source: In addition, the rate of migration for the single centriole that migrates in C. elegans neurons is similar to that of mouse OSN centrioles (in OSNs: maximum of 0.18 µm/min; in C. elegans: 0.076 µm/min, Li et al., 2017), suggesting that similar mechanisms may drive centriole migration in both contexts.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Dynein motors acting processively exhibit velocities of approximately 60 µm/min in cells and in vitro.
claims.source: However, dynein motors acting processively exhibit velocities much higher than those observed in OSNs or the PQR neuron, approximately 60 µm/min in cells and in vitro (Presley et al., 1997; King and Schroer, 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: OSN dendrites have a polarized microtubule cytoskeleton, in which the microtubule minus ends are oriented out, toward the dendritic tips.
claims.source: OSN dendrites have a polarized microtubule cytoskeleton, in which the microtubule minus ends are oriented out, toward the dendritic tips (Burton, 1985).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Microtubule polarity in dendrites of non-ciliated C. elegans PVD neurons is established by a non-centrosomal microtubule organizing center that is present at the dendritic tip.
claims.source: An interesting parallel is that microtubule polarity in dendrites of non-ciliated C. elegans PVD neurons is established by a non-centrosomal microtubule organizing center that is present at the dendritic tip (Liang et al., 2020), suggesting that this may be a conserved mechanism of establishing and maintaining microtubule polarity in dendrites.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

results.result: Progenitor cells contain on average ~26 centrioles, mature OSNs contain ~36 centrioles, and ~85% of centrioles in mature OSNs are associated with cilia (~31 cilia per knob). The majority of centrioles in mature OSNs originate from progenitor cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C37 are supported by expansion microscopy data with quantification (n=20 progenitor cells, n=24 mature OSNs from two mice). Sample sizes are modest but adequate for descriptive quantification. The inference that progenitors form the majority of centrioles (C35) is reasonable given the counts and is supported by prior work.

results.result: Centrioles migrate in multiple groups within a single OSN dendrite during dendrite outgrowth, with more groups found in the apical portion of the epithelium.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C38, C27, C28 are supported by expansion microscopy imaging (Figure 2A) and are consistent with prior TEM observations (Heist and Mulvaney, 1968; Mulvaney and Heist, 1971). The observation of multiple groups per dendrite is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Centriole migration occurs in tandem with dendrite extension. Centriole groups lag behind the dendrite tip by up to 8.4 µm, and microtubules are present both apical and basal to migrating centrioles.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 2B) showing centrioles in partially elongated dendrites with GAP43 and β-tubulin III staining. Sample size (n=12 dendrites, N=2 animals) is adequate for this descriptive observation.

results.result: Centrioles migrate slowly with a maximum rate of 0.18 µm/min. Most groups move apically, but ~1/3 show no net movement or basal movement during imaging. At this rate, centrioles could take >9.26 hr to traverse a 100 µm epithelium.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C43-C45, C89 are supported by live imaging data (n=22 centriole groups, N=3 animals, Figure 2C-D). The calculation in C89 is straightforward arithmetic. The observation of bidirectional or stalled movement is interesting but the imaging window is limited, so net directionality over longer timescales is uncertain.

results.result: Migrating centrioles lack rootletin and are not held together by rootletin-based cohesion fibers. Some centrioles migrate singly. Rootletin is present in mature OSNs.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C49 are supported by expansion microscopy data (Figure 3A). The absence of rootletin on migrating centrioles is clearly shown, and the antibody is validated by positive signal in mature OSNs and tissue culture cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The inference that cohesion fibers are absent (C47) is reasonable.

results.result: STIL and SASS6 are present on amplifying centrioles in progenitors and retained on some migrating centrioles in immature OSNs, but absent in mature OSNs. This suggests immature procentrioles can migrate, while mature OSNs contain mature centrioles lacking these markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C54 are supported by expansion microscopy data (Figures 3B-C). The presence of STIL and SASS6 on migrating centrioles is clearly shown. The inferences (C53-C54) are reasonable given the data, though the exact proportion of migrating centrioles with these markers is not quantified.

results.result: Migrating OSN centrioles are associated with microtubule nucleation proteins (gamma-tubulin, CDK5RAP2, pericentrin) and PCM. In mature OSNs, gamma-tubulin and CDK5RAP2 remain, while pericentrin decreases.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C61 are supported by expansion microscopy data (Figures 3D-F). The presence of PCM proteins on migrating centrioles is clearly demonstrated, distinguishing OSNs from many other neurons. The decrease in pericentrin in mature OSNs is noted but not quantified.

results.result: In immature OSNs near the apical surface with multiple centrioles, a single cilium is present. This cilium is associated with the centriole bearing distal appendages (CEP164), confirming centriole asymmetry. The parental centriole forms a cilium before other centrioles.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64, C12, C71 are supported by expansion microscopy data (Figures 4A, A'). The observation of a single cilium with CEP164 on one centriole is clear. The inference that this is the parental centriole (C71) is reasonable given the context of other data (C11, C68).

results.result: In mature OSNs with multiple cilia, many centrioles acquire distal appendages, indicating centriole maturation and remodeling occur at the apical surface.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66, C10 are supported by expansion microscopy data (Figure 4B). The acquisition of CEP164 by multiple centrioles in mature OSNs is clearly shown. The inference that maturation occurs at the apical surface (C66) is reasonable.

results.result: During migration and amplification, only a single centriole (the parental centriole) has distal and subdistal appendages. Centriole modifications required for ciliogenesis occur after migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C68-C70 are supported by expansion microscopy data (Figures 4C, 4—figure supplement 1A-C). The presence of appendages on a single centriole is clearly shown. The hypothesis (C67) is reasonable and supported by prior work. The inference (C70) is well-supported.

results.result: The parental centriole retains a unique centriolin configuration (radial subdistal appendage pattern) in mature OSNs, while other centrioles have single centriolin foci (basal feet). This unique structural characteristic distinguishes the parental centriole's cilium.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C73-C76 are supported by expansion microscopy data (Figures 4D-E, 4—figure supplement 1B, D). The unique centriolin pattern on one centriole is clearly shown. The inference (C76) is reasonable and consistent with findings in MMCCs (C72).

results.result: A novel air-liquid interface explant culture system was developed. Explants remain viable, synthesize DNA, amplify centrioles, and retain tissue architecture. Paclitaxel treatment (microtubule stabilization) causes accumulation of centriole groups, particularly in the subapical compartment, suggesting microtubule dynamics are required for centriole migration to the apical surface.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C77-C88 are supported by explant culture data (Figures 5B-F). EdU incorporation demonstrates viability. Paclitaxel treatment shows a 2.58-fold increase in subapical centriole groups at 6 hr (p=0.0084 by paired permutation test, N=2 animals). The statistical test is appropriate for paired data. Sample size is limited (N=2) but the effect is consistent and statistically significant. The inference (C88) is reasonable.

results.result: A model is proposed for centriole amplification in OSNs: rosette formation around parental centrioles in progenitors, followed by mitotic division, centriole disengagement, and further amplification in post-mitotic OSNs. This results in centrioles of three different ages in immature OSNs.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C93 represent a model/inference based on the current data and prior work (Ching and Stearns, 2020). The model is parsimonious and consistent with the centriole counts (C33-C35) and the presence of markers of different maturation states (C50-C54). However, it remains a model requiring further validation.

results.result: A portion of amplified centrioles in immature OSNs have undergone centriole-to-centrosome conversion, as evidenced by PCM proteins.
results.evaluation: Claim C94 is an inference supported by the presence of PCM proteins (C55-C61) and citations to prior work on centriole-to-centrosome conversion. The inference is reasonable but the exact proportion is not quantified.

results.result: Final modification of non-parental centrioles with rootlets, distal appendages, and subdistal appendages appears to be controlled spatially/temporally by arrival at the dendritic knob.
results.evaluation: Claim C95 is an inference supported by the observation that these components are absent on migrating centrioles (C46, C10) but present in mature OSNs (C49, C65). The inference is reasonable but the mechanism is not directly tested.

results.result: The presence of a single cilium before formation of multiple cilia might enable signaling important for OSN differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claim C96 is speculation (evidence_type: SPECULATION) based on analogy to MMCCs. The authors note that the earliest OSN cilia lack olfactory receptors (C97), which weakens the signaling hypothesis. No direct evidence is provided.

results.result: OSNs detect odorants using multiple cilia that protrude from the dendrite and require centrioles for formation. Cilia provide specialized membrane for olfactory receptor signaling, and disruption causes anosmia.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C15-C17 are established knowledge supported by citations. These are foundational facts about OSN biology and cilium structure.

results.result: Centrioles in OSNs originate in progenitor cells near the basal lamina (50-100 µm from apical surface). Centriole amplification occurs in mitotically active progenitors before mitotic divisions are completed, which is unique among multiciliated cells. OSN differentiation and maturation follow a well-characterized timeline.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C18-C25 are supported by citations to prior work, including the authors' previous study (Ching and Stearns, 2020) and other established literature. These provide essential context for the current study.

results.result: Prior work has observed migrating centrioles in OSNs by TEM and in C. elegans PQR neurons. Vertebrate OSNs contain multiple centrioles that migrate over greater distances (10-fold) than C. elegans and develop throughout life.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C32 are supported by citations to prior work. These provide context for the novelty of the current study. The 10-fold distance comparison (C31) is a reasonable inference from the stated distances (5 µm vs 50-100 µm).

results.result: Prior work in MMCCs and C. elegans neurons provides relevant comparisons for centriole migration mechanisms, including parental centriole identity, effects of microtubule stabilization, dynein involvement, and microtubule polarity in dendrites.
results.evaluation: Claims C72, C98-C104 are supported by citations to prior work. These provide important context for interpreting the current findings and proposing mechanisms.

results.result: Migrating centrioles are associated with microtubule nucleation factors but acquire rootletin and appendages only in mature OSNs.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9 summarize findings detailed in other claim groups (C55-C61 for nucleation factors, C46-C49 for rootletin, C10, C65 for appendages). These are well-supported by the data.

results.result: Dividing progenitors require multiple days to give rise to fully mature OSNs.
results.evaluation: Claim C90 is supported by citations to prior work (Rodriguez-Gil et al., 2015; McClintock et al., 2020). This provides context for the calculated migration time (C89).
